strengths: Addresses an important problem: unreliable minority-class pseudo-labels in graph self-training. The modular combination of clustering/classifier agreement, ranking fusion, and ambiguity filtering is understandable and applicable across GNN architectures.

The reported evaluation is broad, covering synthetic and natural imbalance, multiple backbones, heterophilous graphs, and large datasets. Some gains are substantial: on CiteSeer with GCN and imbalance ratio 10, Macro-F1 improves from the strongest baseline’s 56.81 to 64.94. Additional pseudo-label accuracy analyses provide useful evidence about selection quality.

A public code link, pseudocode, hyperparameter ranges, hardware descriptions, and repeated-run results provide useful reproducibility support. No material research ethics concerns are apparent from the described benchmark-based study.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect as stated. A minority node can move toward a wrong class center, increasing geometric imbalance while becoming confidently misclassified and reducing entropy. Appendix C also drops the class priors and assumes equal concentration parameters without justification. Its final bounds contradict each other at D_intra = 0, requiring both H >= log C and H <= log C - κ/(2C²) for κ > 0. These are substantive failures of the central theoretical contribution.

Theorem 2 conflates labeled-class imbalance with neighborhood composition. Under the stated fixed extractor and class centers, changing which majority nodes are labeled can change ρ without changing minority embeddings or their geometric imbalance. No graph-generating assumptions justify the asserted increase in cross-class neighbor influence. The proof additionally switches from proportionality to ρ² to proportionality to ρ without justification. Experiments that retrain the encoder do not validate this fixed-extractor claim.

The connection between the theory and algorithm remains unestablished. The formal score measures distance to the true class center relative to global class separation, whereas DGIS uses a nearest-two-centroid distance gap. No approximation guarantee or direct empirical correspondence is demonstrated. Theorem 3 establishes only properties of the ranking weights, not reduced geometric imbalance or improved selection. Moreover, confidence weight min(r, 1-r) increases only until r = 0.5.

The downstream ablations contradict their interpretation. As printed, Tables 1 and 32 mark both Node-Reordering and DGIS as absent in the best-performing row of every setting, and contain no row with all components enabled. Nevertheless, the text claims their combination performs best in three settings. Corrected tables and clearly specified configurations are necessary to establish which components produce the reported gains.

Methodological originality is insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Appendix B describes M3S as already using clustering alignment to filter classifier pseudo-labels, closely overlapping DPAM. Its comparison is restricted to CS-Random without uncertainty estimates, while the directly relevant, cited IceBerg method is not evaluated. Comparisons under severe imbalance and against simpler ranking-fusion rules would better establish the incremental contribution.

Experimental reporting contains material inconsistencies. Tables 7 and 17 report different ogbn-arxiv results for UNREAL, including GCN F1 of 50.65 versus 50.32. Claims of consistent superiority overlook failures such as Computers-Random with GraphSAGE, where balanced accuracy and F1 trail the strongest baseline by 3.17 and 1.73 points. The checklist also describes standard deviations while most tables specify standard errors.

The efficiency evidence does not establish total computational cost. Table 12 times fixed training blocks and individual selection operations on small graphs, while Appendix K permits 40–100 self-training rounds with up to 2,000 epochs per round. End-to-end runtime and peak memory on large graphs, together with complete dataset-specific configurations, are needed to substantiate scalability and facilitate replication. Overall, the theoretical failures and unresolved experimental inconsistencies outweigh the promising reported gains.
